The Southern cassowary (Casuarius casuarius) is the largest avian frugivore of the Australasian rainforests, and its life history traits reflect a strategy of slow development and substantial parental investment. Under the thermal conditions typical of the incubating nest environment (34 °C [T = 34 °C]), the incubation period extends to approximately 50 days [ab = approximately 50 days], a duration that is consistent with the large egg size characteristic of this species. The developing embryo is maintained at an optimal temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] during incubation, a figure that has been adopted as a general reference for embryonic development in many birds in the absence of species-specific data. Upon hatching, the precocial chick emerges with a wet weight at birth of 413 grams [Wwb = 413 grams], though field records compiled by Rome (1997) indicate a range of 402 to 499 grams for neonatal mass. This substantial initial mass permits the chick to be mobile and to follow the adult male almost immediately after emergence, a key adaptation for survival in the predator-rich forest floor environment.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is pronounced in this species, with females attaining a considerably larger ultimate wet weight for females of 58.5 kilograms [Wwi = 58.5 kilograms], although maximum recorded individuals have been documented at up to 85 kilograms under optimal foraging conditions. In contrast, the male reaches an ultimate wet weight for males of 31 kilograms [Wwi = 31 kilograms], with field reports indicating a typical range between 29 and 34 kilograms for fully grown territorial males. This marked disparity in adult body mass is among the most extreme within the Palaeognathae and is thought to be linked to the species' polyandrous mating system, where larger females compete for access to multiple males who then assume sole responsibility for incubation and chick rearing. The considerable energetic demands of producing large eggs and maintaining competitive dominance over preferred territories likely drive the selective pressures favoring this substantial female size.

The reproductive phenology of the Southern cassowary is characterized by a low annual output, consistent with its position as a long-lived, slow-breeding species. Females produce between 4 and 8 eggs per season [Ri = between 4 and 8 eggs per season], and typically complete only a single nesting event each year [F_R_i = single nesting event each year]. These values, recorded at the species' active body temperature of 38.17 °C [T = 38.17 °C], represent a modest reproductive rate even by ratite standards. The eggs are large and vividly colored, ranging from bright green to turquoise, and each represents a significant energetic investment for the female. Clutch size appears to be influenced by the nutritional condition of the female prior to the breeding season, with years of high fruit abundance correlating with the upper end of the range. The male incubates the clutch alone for approximately 50 days, during which he rarely leaves the nest and relies entirely on stored body reserves.

Development from hatching to independence proceeds through a series of well-defined milestones that reflect the species' extended period of juvenile dependency. Under the thermal conditions typical of a homeothermic adult (38.17 °C [T = 38.17 °C]), fledging—marked by the attainment of full juvenile plumage and the ability to escape predators by running—occurs at approximately 275 days after hatching [tx = approximately 275 days after hatching]. This is followed by a lengthy period of association with the adult male, with puberty estimated at approximately 488 days after hatching [tp = approximately 488 days after hatching], a value based on the observation that young birds typically reach independence from the father after a at a temperature of 38.17 °C [T = 38.17 °C]bout 16 months. The first successful breeding event, or time since birth at first brood, is deferred until approximately 1,095 days after hatching [tR = approximately 1,095 days after hatching], underscoring the considerable time required for a young cassowary to acquire the body size, foraging proficiency, and social standing necessary to secure a territory and at a temperature of 38.17 °C [T = 38.17 °C]attract a mate.

Longevity in the Southern cassowary is considerable for a bird of its body size, with the maximum lifespan estimated at approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] under field conditions at 38.17 °C [T = 38.17 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with deferred maturity and low annual reproductive output, positions the species at the extreme slow end of the life-history continuum among birds. The species' reliance on large, spatially dispersed fruiting trees for food may impose a constraint on population density and juvenile survival, as young birds must navigate a complex social landscape to establish their own territories. Comparative analyses indicate that this longevity is comparable to that of other large ratites such as the emu and the greater rhea, although the cassowary's more restricted habitat and higher vulnerability to habitat fragmentation may limit the realization of its full lifespan potential in anthropogenically altered landscapes.
